title: Argument writing: claims, evidence and counterclaims
summary: Students sort evidence on whether middle school should start later, then write a short argument with a claim, relevant evidence, commentary and a rebuttal to a counterclaim.

standard.text: Write arguments to support claims with clear reasons and relevant evidence.

discourse: Organize an argument so each reason is followed by evidence and by commentary that explains how the evidence proves the reason.
Acknowledge a counterclaim fairly, then answer it with a rebuttal instead of ignoring it.
Choose relevant, credible evidence and leave out facts that are interesting but do not support the claim.
sentence: Concession structures: Although some people believe ___, ___. While it is true that ___, ___.
Introducing a source with a reporting verb: According to ___, ___. A survey by ___ shows that ___.
Modal verbs that set the strength of a claim: should, must, could, might.
word: Reporting verbs with different meanings: states, shows, reports, suggests, argues.
Argument transitions: furthermore, in addition, however, on the other hand, therefore.
Words that signal opinion versus fact: I believe, it seems, clearly versus data show, researchers found.

contentObjective: Students will write an argument that states a claim about school start times and supports it with clear reasons, relevant evidence and a rebuttal to a counterclaim.
languageObjective: Students will argue in writing using a reporting verb to introduce evidence (According to ___, ___ or ___ shows that ___) and a concession structure (Although ___, ___) to respond to a counterclaim.

L1-2: I think school should start ___. (later / at the same time)
L5-6: The strongest reason to ___ is ___, as shown by ___.
This evidence matters because it demonstrates that ___, which means ___.
Opponents may argue that ___; however, this concern overlooks ___.
While ___ is a fair point, a better solution would be ___ because ___.

vocabulary.definition: the main position a writer argues for and tries to prove
facts, data, examples or expert statements that support a reason
a position that disagrees with the writer's claim
the part of an argument that answers a counterclaim and shows why the claim is still stronger
closely connected to the point being made
able to be trusted or believed
to admit that something is true or deserves attention
vocabulary.morphology: a- + knowledge: to show you know about something

vocabulary.definition: to convince someone to believe or do something

activity.title: Evidence Sort and Build
steps: Pose the question: 'Should our middle school start one hour later?' Students take a 30-second stand by writing yes or no on scrap paper.

Write four pieces of evidence on the board (sample information written for this lesson): A) In a survey of 200 students at one school, 140 said they feel sleepy in first period. B) Doctors recommend that people ages 13 to 18 get 8 to 10 hours of sleep. C) The school's soccer team won four games this fall. D) A later start could push after-school practices and jobs later into the evening.

Partners sort the evidence into relevant to yes, relevant to no and not relevant, and explain each choice aloud with 'Evidence ___ is relevant because ___.' (C is not relevant; D supports the no side, so a yes writer can use it as the counterclaim.)
Partners solve the problem below so they can state the survey result as a percent in their writing.
Each student writes a paragraph: claim, one reason, evidence introduced with According to or shows that, one or two sentences of commentary, then a concession sentence (Although ___) and a rebuttal.
Pairs swap paragraphs and underline the reporting verb and circle the concession word. If either is missing, the writer revises one sentence before sharing.

problems.prompt: In evidence A, 140 of 200 surveyed students said they feel sleepy in first period. What percent of the students is that?

warmup: Strong or Weak? Read two short arguments aloud on a familiar topic, for example: 'We should have more recess because it is fun' and 'We should have more recess because a short break can help students focus when they return to class.' Students show thumbs up for the stronger one, then a partner explains why using: 'The second one is stronger because it gives a reason that ___.'
